title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 56–57 (editorially reviewed)
description: Units 56–57 checked against the illustrated teaching pages, exercises and answer key. Unit 56 covers positive and negative evaluative adjectives and natural reactions. Unit 57 covers verbs and adjectives with prepositions, look combinations, and noun/-ing complements. Examples and English notes are original; Brazilian Portuguese is used only in pt; pronunciation uses British English IPA.
sourceNotice: The supplied textbook was used to check instructional targets, diagrams, classroom examples and exercises. Examples and explanations are original. Dictionary guidance for Unit 56 exercise words and grammatical examples extending Unit 57 are identified in item notes.

audit.scope: Inspected Unit 56 teaching sections A–C, illustrations and exercises 56.1–56.5 and Unit 57 teaching sections A–D, look diagram, exercises 57.1–57.5 and the Common mistakes box; compared the published answer key on printed pp. 155–156 (PDF pp. 156–157). Reviewed all 100 entries for English text, contextual meaning, Brazilian Portuguese translations and British IPA.
audit.pronunciation: British English IPA, mainly non-rhotic, checked entry by entry against British reference forms and the phonetic notation shown in the textbook. Multiword expressions may vary in stress and weak forms in connected speech.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Local JSON parsing and structure, ID preservation, language checks and item review do not constitute an application test. VocabLab 1.2 Lite import, browser text-to-speech, recording, spaced-repetition behaviour and backup/restore have not been tested. Human approval is outstanding.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Compared source teaching text, illustrations, diagrams, exercises and published answer key; reviewed each item for phonetics, meaning, spelling, examples and English-only content; ran local JSON/ID/type validation.
editorialReview.notes: All 100 existing vocabulary item IDs and both unit IDs are preserved. Provenance: the targets look forward to seeing you, afraid of flying and thank someone for helping are educational examples applying source patterns, not phrases listed verbatim in the teaching pages. All other entries refer to source vocabulary or source-reinforced structures.

units.title: Unit 56 — Common adjectives: Good and bad things
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 56, printed pp. 118–119 (PDF pp. 119–120); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: This is a good place to have lunch.
items.note: Good is a general positive adjective. Nice, lovely, great, wonderful and excellent also express approval; the strength of each depends on context.

items.example: You have a nice garden.
items.note: Nice expresses a favourable opinion of people, places and things; a nice jacket is a phrase on the teaching page.

items.example: We had a lovely afternoon by the sea.
items.note: Lovely is a warm, positive adjective, especially common in British English. It can also stand alone as a positive response.

items.example: That was a great match.
items.note: Great conveys enthusiasm or strong approval. It can describe a film or serve as a short response: Great!

items.example: The children had a wonderful holiday.
items.note: Wonderful expresses strong approval or delight. The source illustrates a wonderful view and the response Wonderful!

items.example: Your presentation was excellent.
items.note: Excellent means extremely good. The teaching page contrasts a good restaurant and an excellent restaurant.

items.example: The new café is very good.
items.note: Very intensifies good. The textbook presents these positive adjectives on a broad scale rather than as perfectly interchangeable synonyms.

items.example: There is a good restaurant near the market.
items.note: Good describes the restaurant's quality. Both restaurant photographs appear in the teaching section.

items.example: We found an excellent restaurant by the harbour.
items.note: Use an before excellent because the next word starts with a vowel sound; compare a good restaurant.

items.example: Our flat has a wonderful view of the river.
items.note: A wonderful view is a natural collocation for an impressive scene; the noun view often takes of + place or object.

items.pt: uma jaqueta bonita; um casaco bonito
items.example: I bought a nice jacket for winter.
items.note: Nice is a common way to compliment someone's clothes. The textbook uses this phrase in a short dialogue.

items.pt: um dia adorável; um dia lindo
items.example: It was a lovely day for a picnic.
items.note: A lovely day conveys an enjoyable or pleasant day, often with fine weather. The page presents it in a short dialogue.

items.example: We watched a great film yesterday.
items.note: Film is a normal British English word for a movie. Great gives an enthusiastic evaluation.

items.example: Taking the earlier bus is an excellent idea.
items.note: An excellent idea expresses enthusiastic approval of a suggestion. The article is an before excellent.

items.example: I had a bad meal at the airport.
items.note: Bad expresses a negative judgment. Dreadful, horrible and terrible are stronger alternatives in the teaching section.

items.pt: muito ruim; muito mau; muito má
items.example: The service was very bad yesterday.
items.note: Very bad is an intensified negative evaluation; the book gives dreadful, horrible and terrible as alternatives.

items.example: The hotel had a dreadful smell.
items.note: Dreadful means extremely bad or unpleasant. The source uses it to describe a smell; exercise 56.4 reviews it.

items.example: I had a horrible journey in the rain.
items.note: Horrible means extremely unpleasant. The teaching page uses horrible food and the reaction How horrible!

items.example: Traffic was terrible on our way home.
items.note: Terrible means very bad or unpleasant; the teaching page applies it to a day and to heavy traffic.

items.example: I feel awful after so little sleep.
items.note: Awful is a strong negative adjective, used for an unpleasant experience or appearance; it also appears in How awful!

items.example: We stayed indoors because of bad weather.
items.note: Weather is normally uncountable in this meaning: bad weather, not a bad weather.

items.example: They served horrible food at the event.
items.note: Horrible describes the food in the teaching example. Food can be uncountable when referring to food generally.

items.example: There was a dreadful smell in the corridor.
items.note: Smell is countable here, so a dreadful smell is correct. Dreadful intensifies a negative evaluation.

items.example: She had a terrible day at school.
items.note: A terrible day describes an especially unpleasant day, as in the teaching example about work.

items.example: There is terrible traffic near the stadium today.
items.note: Traffic is normally uncountable in this meaning. The source uses terrible traffic for very busy roads.

items.example: “The tickets are ready.” “Excellent!”
items.note: Excellent! is a complete, enthusiastic response to a favourable plan or piece of news in the source dialogue.

items.example: “I can meet you on Friday.” “Great!”
items.note: Great! is a natural, brief response of approval; it does not need a following noun.

items.example: “We passed the exam!” “Wonderful!”
items.note: Wonderful! expresses pleasure or excitement about something positive in the source dialogue.

items.example: “Shall we have tea outside?” “Lovely!”
items.note: Lovely! is a warm expression of approval, particularly frequent in British English conversation.

items.example: “I will arrive at six.” “Perfect!”
items.note: Perfect! indicates that a plan, arrangement or proposed time suits the speaker exactly.

items.example: “How was your interview?” “Not bad!”
items.note: Not bad often means reasonably good or better than expected rather than literally bad; tone and context matter.

items.pt: Nada mal!; Até que é bom!
items.example: “I finished the test in twenty minutes.” “That’s not bad!”
items.note: That's not bad! can express mild praise or approval. In the source, it is a favourable response to someone's weekly pay.

items.example: “My wallet was stolen.” “How awful!”
items.note: How awful! is a reaction to bad news. The Common mistakes box discourages How bad! for this function.

items.example: “Our train was cancelled again.” “How horrible!”
items.note: How horrible! reacts sympathetically to something unpleasant. Use How + adjective! to express a reaction.

items.example: “My brother is coming to visit.” “How nice!”
items.note: How nice! is a friendly reaction to positive news. The source contrasts it with reactions to bad news.

items.example: “We are having a baby!” “How wonderful!”
items.note: How wonderful! expresses enthusiastic delight about positive news, such as a new job.

items.example: “They gave me flowers.” “How lovely!”
items.note: How lovely! is an affectionate, positive reaction and follows the same How + adjective pattern.

items.example: Your plan sounds brilliant.
items.note: Brilliant is placed in the good column by exercise 56.4. Its positive meaning and example are supporting dictionary-style guidance.

items.example: We had a marvellous time on holiday.
items.note: Marvellous is a strongly positive adjective from exercise 56.4; the spelling marvellous is British English (US marvelous).

items.example: There was a nasty taste in the water.
items.note: Nasty is a negative adjective in exercise 56.4. It can mean unpleasant, unkind or disagreeable depending on context.

items.example: The weather was fine for our walk.
items.note: Fine is classified as positive in exercise 56.4. It often means satisfactory or pleasant, but is not always as emphatic as excellent.

items.example: We had awful weather on our camping trip.
items.note: Awful weather is a negative collocation tested in exercise 56.3. Weather takes no indefinite article in this sense.

items.example: We enjoyed lovely weather all weekend.
items.note: Lovely weather is a positive weather description paired with sunshine in exercise 56.3.

items.example: That is wonderful news about your sister.
items.note: Wonderful news is a positive collocation in exercise 56.3. News is an uncountable noun that takes a singular verb.

items.example: They booked an excellent hotel in the centre.
items.note: An excellent hotel is the five-star example in exercise 56.3. An precedes the vowel sound in excellent.

items.example: Taking a break now is a very good idea.
items.note: A very good idea describes a strong, positive suggestion, as in the matching activity 56.3.

items.example: There is a lovely house near the beach.
items.note: A lovely house expresses admiration. Exercise 56.1 describes a house close to the sea.

learningObjectives: Recognise common positive adjectives (good, nice, lovely, great, wonderful and excellent) and their shades of approval.
Use negative evaluations (bad, dreadful, horrible, terrible and awful) in everyday situations.
Combine adjectives naturally with restaurant, view, idea, weather, food, smell, traffic and similar nouns.
Respond appropriately with Excellent!, Great!, Lovely!, Perfect! and other short positive reactions.
Understand how not bad can express a moderately favourable evaluation.
React with How + adjective! and avoid the inappropriate How bad! response highlighted in the source.
Classify brilliant, marvellous, nasty and fine as positive or negative, then use them with suitable nouns, as prompted by exercises 56.4–56.5.

units.title: Unit 57 — Words and prepositions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 57, printed pp. 120–121 (PDF pp. 121–122); original example sentences.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: We listen to music while we cook.
items.note: Listen usually takes to before its object: listen to music, not listen music. The book illustrates listen to the radio.

items.example: My grandfather likes to listen to the radio in the kitchen.
items.note: The teaching page uses listen to the radio in the morning. The noun radio usually has the in this expression.

items.example: Please wait for me outside the shop.
items.note: Use wait for + person or thing awaited, such as wait for the bus; wait alone is possible without an object.

items.example: We waited for the bus after school.
items.note: Wait for the bus means remain until the bus arrives. The source also practises wait for a train.

items.example: I asked for a glass of water.
items.note: Use ask for when requesting something, such as food or drink. Contrast ask someone a question.

items.example: He asked for a coffee at the café.
items.note: Ask for a coffee is a natural request in a café. The teaching page specifically contrasts black and white coffee.

items.example: Who will pay for the tickets?
items.note: Pay for + item or service means give money to obtain it. The source practises pay for a meal and tickets.

items.example: She offered to pay for our meal.
items.note: Pay for a meal identifies what the payment covers. The question in the book is Where do I pay for our meal?

items.example: Can you come to my house tomorrow?
items.note: Come to introduces a destination or event, as in come to my party. The preposition is part of the illustrated pattern.

items.pt: vir a uma festa; comparecer a uma festa
items.example: Many neighbours came to our party.
items.note: Come to a party means attend or visit a social event. The teaching text uses come to my party.

items.example: This umbrella belongs to Helen.
items.note: Belong to can express ownership or membership: This book belongs to Sarah; she belongs to a club.

items.pt: pertencer a um clube; ser membro de um clube
items.example: My sister belongs to a sports club.
items.note: Belong to a club describes membership; the textbook tests it in exercise 57.3 and in a personal question.

items.example: I often think about my old school.
items.note: Think about means direct your thoughts to someone or something. Exercise 57.1 uses thinking about the holidays.

items.pt: agradecer a alguém por alguma coisa
items.example: I thanked my neighbour for the help.
items.note: Use thank + person + for + reason: thank someone for a present. A verb after for takes -ing.

items.pt: agradecer a alguém por um presente
items.example: Mia thanked her friend for the present.
items.note: The person follows thank directly; for introduces the gift or other reason for thanking them.

items.example: I apologised for the mistake.
items.note: Apologise for is British spelling. Use apologise for + noun or -ing form; past tense apologised.

items.example: They apologised for being late to class.
items.note: For is a preposition in apologise for being late, so being is the appropriate -ing form.

items.example: Look at this picture, please.
items.note: Look at directs attention to an object. Contrast look for, which means search for an object.

items.pt: olhar um livro; examinar um livro
items.example: The child likes to look at picture books.
items.note: Look at a book means observe its pages or pictures. The source's diagram connects look at with a book.

items.example: I am looking for my glasses.
items.note: Look for means try to find something that is missing or wanted, such as keys or a job.

items.example: We looked for a key under the sofa.
items.note: Look for a key means search for it. The diagram uses a key to contrast look for and look at.

items.example: My aunt looks after our dog on Fridays.
items.note: Look after means take care of a person, animal or thing; the textbook uses it with children.

items.example: My neighbour looks after the children after school.
items.note: Look after the children means care for them; after does not refer only to a position or later time.

items.pt: aguardar com expectativa; estar ansioso(a) por
items.example: I am looking forward to my holiday next month.
items.note: Look forward to means anticipate a pleasant future event. The to here is a preposition, followed by a noun or -ing verb.

items.example: We are looking forward to the party on Saturday.
items.note: Look forward to the party expresses pleasure about a forthcoming event. The source diagram uses a party.

items.pt: estar ansioso(a) para ver você; aguardar com expectativa o encontro
items.example: I look forward to seeing you next week.
items.note: This extends the source pattern with a following -ing verb: look forward to seeing someone, not look forward to see someone.

items.example: She is looking for a new job this month.
items.note: Look for a new job is directly practised in exercise 57.2. For identifies what someone wants to find.

items.example: Please look at me when we talk.
items.note: Look at me is directly practised in exercise 57.2. Me is the object pronoun after at.

items.example: He is good at science.
items.note: Be good at + subject, sport or -ing form describes a skill: good at geography; good at playing the piano.

items.pt: ruim em; não ter habilidade para
items.example: I am bad at drawing.
items.note: Be bad at + subject, sport or -ing form describes difficulty or weak performance in a skill.

items.example: My mother is interested in history.
items.note: Be interested in + noun or -ing form describes something that interests you. Do not substitute interested on here.

items.example: My younger brother is afraid of dogs.
items.note: Be afraid of introduces a source of fear, including an activity in its -ing form: afraid of flying.

items.example: Her parents are proud of her.
items.note: Be proud of introduces a person, achievement or action, including proud of winning.

items.example: I am used to busy streets.
items.note: Be used to + noun/-ing form means something is already familiar. Contrast past-habit used to + base verb.

items.example: You will get used to the new timetable.
items.note: Get used to + noun/-ing form describes becoming familiar with something new, rather than already being comfortable with it.

items.example: We are happy about the good news.
items.note: Be happy about + event or success describes satisfaction. The source rejects happy for her success in this context.

items.example: I am interested in hearing your idea.
items.note: Interested in hearing illustrates a preposition followed by an -ing form, not the base verb hear.

items.pt: orgulhoso(a) de vencer; orgulhoso(a) por ter conquistado algo
items.example: She is proud of winning her first match.
items.note: Proud of winning describes feeling pleased about an achievement. After of, use the -ing form winning.

items.example: I am used to getting up early for work.
items.note: Be used to getting up early describes a familiar present routine; past-habit used to get up has a different meaning.

items.example: It took him time to get used to driving in the city.
items.note: Get used to driving describes an adaptation process. After to, the verb is in the -ing form.

items.example: My friend is afraid of mice.
items.note: Afraid of mice uses an irregular plural: mouse becomes mice. It appears in the teaching examples.

items.example: Her coach was happy about her success.
items.note: The Common mistakes box uses happy about her success, not happy for her success in this meaning.

items.pt: bom(boa) em tênis; jogar tênis bem
items.example: I am good at tennis but not at football.
items.note: At is followed by a noun in good at tennis. Exercise 57.5 asks learners about their own skills.

items.example: My brother is good at playing the piano.
items.note: At is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing in good at playing the piano, as explained in section D.

items.example: My aunt is afraid of flying.
items.note: Afraid of flying is an added example of the source's preposition + -ing rule; it is not a separately listed headword on the teaching page.

items.example: We are interested in sport.
items.note: Interested in sport is practised in exercise 57.3. Sport is the noun following in.

items.word: get used to a new school
items.example: Emma quickly got used to her new school.
items.note: The textbook introduces get used to a new school and practises got used to her new school in exercise 57.3.

items.example: The trip is next month, and I look forward to it.
items.note: Look forward to it is tested in exercise 57.2. It is the object of to and refers to a future event.

items.example: Her grandmother is very proud of her.
items.note: Proud of her is directly taught and reinforced in exercise 57.3. Her is an object pronoun following of.

items.pt: feliz por ter ganho uma medalha; contente com uma medalha
items.example: He was happy about his medal.
items.note: Happy about a medal illustrates happy about + reason; exercise 57.3 uses happy about her medal.

items.word: used to driving on the left
items.example: The visitor was used to driving on the left.
items.note: Used to driving on the left is practised in exercise 57.4. It means driving on the left was already familiar.

items.pt: não estar acostumado(a) à comida britânica
items.example: At first, the student was not used to British food.
items.note: Not used to British food is practised in exercise 57.4. The negative indicates the food was unfamiliar.

items.example: I thanked my friend for helping me.
items.note: Thank someone for helping extends the source's thank + person + for pattern with an -ing verb.

learningObjectives: Use listen to, wait for, ask for, pay for, come to and belong to with appropriate complements.
Use think about, thank someone for and apologise for, retaining the required person, reason or object.
Distinguish look at, look for, look after and look forward to according to context.
Combine adjectives with their appropriate prepositions: good at, bad at, interested in, afraid of, proud of and happy about.
Distinguish be used to (a familiar situation) from get used to (the process of becoming familiar).
Use a noun or an -ing verb form after a preposition: good at tennis, good at playing, interested in hearing and used to driving.
Apply the Common mistakes warning: happy about her success, not happy for her success in this context.
Practise the combinations in realistic personal responses, including looking forward to an event and belonging to clubs.
